introduction.p: A function assigns one output to each allowed input. For example, a time can determine a position, a radius can determine an area, and a step size can determine an approximation error. We will specify both the assignment and the set of inputs on which it is defined.

subsection.title: Input, output, domain, and range
subsection.p: Imagine a trip along a straight road. At each time t, the car has a position s(t). The input is time. The output is position.

This formula assigns one position to each time.

subsection.p: The word “assigns” is important. A function is not merely a formula. It is a rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input.

statement.p: A function f from a set D to the real numbers is a rule that assigns to each input x\in D exactly one real number f(x).
The set D is called the domain of f.
The set of all outputs is called the range of f:

exercise.title: Why is a formula not yet a function?

statement.p: The formulas f(x)=x^2 on \mathbb R and g(x)=x^2 on [-1,1] look the same, but they are different functions. In your own words, what extra information besides a formula does a function need, and why can two functions share a formula yet have different ranges?

hint.p: A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. Changing the allowed inputs can change the set of outputs that actually appear.

subsection.title: Functions from formulas, graphs, tables, and words
subsection.p: A formula is the most familiar way to describe a function, but it is not the only way.

paragraphs.title: A function from a formula
paragraphs.p: The area A of a circle depends on its radius r:
If the radius is measured in centimeters, then the area is measured in square centimeters. The natural domain is
because a radius cannot be negative.

paragraphs.title: A function from a table
paragraphs.p: A thermometer may record the temperature of a cup of tea every minute.
This table defines a function on the domain
For example,
The table does not tell us the exact temperature at t=2.5. It may suggest one, but it does not assign one unless we add more information.
This distinction will matter later. Data can suggest a model, but the model is a new function.

paragraphs.title: A function from a graph
paragraphs.p: A graph can also describe a function. The input x is read along the horizontal axis. The output f(x) is read along the vertical axis.

A graph represents a function only when each input gives exactly one output. This is the reason for the vertical line test: a vertical line corresponds to one input x. If it hits a curve in two places, then that input has two possible outputs, so the curve is not the graph of a function of x.

figure.caption: The full circle gives two y-values for many x-values. The upper semicircle gives exactly one.

description.p: The full circle gives two y-values for many x-values. The upper semicircle gives exactly one.

paragraphs.p: The circle

But the upper semicircle

exercise.title: What can a table remember, and what can it not?

statement.p: A function can come from a formula, a graph, a table, or words. In your own words, what information does a table of temperatures at whole-number minutes actually assign, and why does that table not automatically tell you the temperature at t=2.5?

hint.p: A function only has to answer for inputs in its domain. Ask whether 2.5 is one of the recorded inputs, or an extra interpolation you might be tempted to invent.

subsection.title: The natural domain of a formula
subsection.p: When a formula is given without an explicit domain, we usually take the domain to be all real numbers for which the formula makes sense. This is called the natural domain.

exercise.title: What does a natural domain protect?

statement.p: When a formula is given without an explicit domain, we take the natural domain: all real inputs for which the formula makes sense. In your own words, what kinds of operations forbid inputs, and why is the natural domain part of the meaning of the formula rather than an afterthought?

hint.p: Think about division by zero and even roots of negative numbers. A formula cannot assign an output where those operations fail.

subsection.title: Piecewise-defined functions
subsection.p: Many real processes follow one rule for a while and then another rule later.

A car may move forward, stop at a light, then reverse into a parking space. A tax bill may use one rate for the first part of income and another rate for the next part. A postage cost may stay constant over a range of weights, then jump.
These functions are often described piece by piece.

exercise.title: Why must a piecewise rule assign a boundary point only once?

statement.p: A piecewise formula that assigns both 1 and 2 at x=0 does not define a function. In your own words, why is exactly one output nonnegotiable, and why does calculus care about the exact value at a boundary between pieces?

hint.p: Nearby behavior is not the same as the value at the joining point. Limits later watch that neighborhood, so the assignment at the endpoint must be unambiguous.

subsection.p: Chapter 1 already used expressions such as
This is an average velocity over a short interval. It is also a new function built from the old function s.
For a general function f, a base input a, and a nonzero step h, define
This is called a difference quotient.
The input a tells us where we start. The input h tells us how far we step. The output is the average rate of change from a to a+h.
The condition
is necessary because division by 0 is not allowed.
There is another domain condition too: both a and a+h must be in the domain of f.

exercise.title: What two inputs does a difference quotient need?

statement.p: The difference quotient Q_f(a,h)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is a new function built from f. In your own words, what do the inputs a and h mean, and why is h\neq0 part of the domain rather than a minor inconvenience?

hint.p: One input names the starting place. The other names the step. Division by zero is not allowed, and both endpoints of the step must lie in the domain of f.

example.title: domain restrictions in the difference quotient
example.p: So the difference quotient has a domain of its own. It is not enough to say “h\neq 0.” We must also keep both inputs of f legal.

note.title: Why this matters
note.p: The derivative will come from the difference quotient by letting h move toward 0. Before taking that limit, we need to know where the quotient is defined.

subsection.p: Functions let one quantity depend on another. Graphs let us see that dependence all at once. Before we can study limits on graphs, we need to learn how graphs move, stretch, reflect, and reveal information.
